title: F1 Drivers Speak Out After the FIA Finally Explains the Bahrain GP Software Crash
description: The FIA has officially concluded its investigation into the chaotic software failure that brought the relocated 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix to a sudden, crawling halt. According to the governing body, a massive coding bug was triggered when cars dropped to…
fullText:
The FIA has officially concluded its investigation into the chaotic software failure that brought the relocated 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix to a sudden, crawling halt. According to the governing body, a massive coding bug was triggered when cars dropped to low engine RPMs inside specific track sectors where a 250kW power reduction was mandated for the wet-weather conditions. This specific combination caused the cars to permanently lose power until the FIA rushed an emergency code update to the grid.

While the unprecedented digital blackout frustrated fans, the drivers actually sitting behind the steering wheels offered a surprisingly nuanced perspective ahead of the Singapore Grand Prix Sprint weekend.

During the official media day at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, drivers were asked by Nelson Valkenburg (Via Play) if they finally feel in control of the complex 2026 engine regulations after the disastrous Sepang incident. For Haas F1 Team driver Esteban Ocon, the Malaysia failure was just a minor bump in the road compared to the absolute nightmare of early-season testing.

"I think, honestly, compared to testing, things have changed, you know, so much," Esteban Ocon explained. "I remember testing the first time I drove the car…. had no deployment. 80% of the laps that I was doing in Barcelona, it was, you know, quite complicated. And we didn't really understand why that was happening."

(Photo by Joe Portlock/LAT Images) // Getty Images / Red Bull Content Pool // SI202610040284 // Usage for editorial use only //

When reflecting specifically on the formation lap chaos at the Sepang Circuit, Esteban Ocon admitted the sudden loss of power was highly confusing, prompting him to try and manually trick the engine into delivering forward momentum.

"This was unexpected for everyone," Esteban Ocon stated. "I started to feel like, yeah, I'm racing because, you know, I was just cutting the lines, trying to do the last metres. I was thinking of maybe upshifting to second, staying on idle to, you know, get more speed compared to the others."

Despite the chaos, he expressed confidence in the governing body, adding, "I'm sure the FIA is on top of it now, so it should be okay."

Alpine F1 Team driver Franco Colapinto echoed those exact sentiments, noting that the entire paddock has been forced to adapt to the wildly unpredictable nature of the 2026 power units.

"I think during the whole year, it improved a lot. It was very inconsistent at the start. It was tricky for everyone to understand," Franco Colapinto told reporters.

He emphasized that massive technical overhauls always come with unexpected growing pains, regardless of how much simulator preparation is completed.

"I think, again, problems and issues we'll still get, and things that we don't know and understand will still happen," Franco Colapinto noted. "But the important thing is we learn from it and get on top of what happened last week, for example."

(Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images) // Getty Images / Red Bull Content Pool // SI202610040283 // Usage for editorial use only //

For seasoned veterans like Aston Martin driver Fernando Alonso, the digital drama was practically a non-issue. Because the Aston Martin garage managed to avoid the wet-weather glitch entirely, the two-time champion was completely unfazed by the software panic.

"In our case, last week, the car was fine," Fernando Alonso shrugged. "So we didn't suffer any of the issues. So difficult to comment." He added that the entire grid now expects the problem to be fully understood and resolved moving forward.

To ensure the multi-million-dollar grid doesn't crash again, the FIA confirmed that the emergency code configuration utilized in Malaysia will remain fully active for the Singapore Grand Prix. A permanent, fully tested wet-weather software patch is scheduled to be released ahead of the United States Grand Prix in Austin later this October.

fullText:
Latest model is launching in New York to target rich US buyers – and is more than 5.2 metres long and 2 metres wide

It has no rear window, will not fit into a UK parking space and – starting at £130,000 – ($172,000) is aimed squarely at rich tech industry buyers driving the wide open roads of America.

Jaguar’s electric car, the Type 01, was launched in New York on Tuesday night and marks the culmination of a two-year rebrand that has been one of the most scrutinised in automotive history.

Bosses hope the vehicle will appeal to a younger, richer audience than the manufacturer’s previous “shrinking and ageing” customer base of “men in their 50s”, said Rawdon Glover, 58, Jaguar’s managing director.

With an ultra-long bonnet, low roof and muscular design, the Type 01 is a sharp departure from its predecessor, the F-Type. It is also double the F-Type’s starting price of about £62,000.

Buyers are likely to be rich, “urban” and “very design literate, very technology literate”, Glover said. “The person making this purchase will be choosing the car because it’s a bold choice.”

A senior JLR executive close to the Type 01 project put it more bluntly: “It’s the type of car that you park up and everybody stops and says: ‘Fucking hell, what have you just turned up in?’”

The launch comes at a critical juncture for parent company Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), which has grappled with falling sales as cheaper Chinese rivals eat into its UK market share. It is still recovering from a massive cyber-attack last year that cost the economy an estimated £1.9bn.

JLR recently announced 4,000 job cuts in an attempt to save £1.7bn over two years, citing “intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”. The Guardian understands Jaguar employees working on the Type 01 programme were offered voluntary redundancy along with the rest of JLR’s non-manufacturing workforce.

The car will go on sale in early 2027, with the first deliveries anticipated in the second half of the year.

“It’s really important that we put Jaguar back on a more solid financial footing,” Glover said. Asked if doubling prices would be effective, he said it was better than “to toil away as we have done for the last two decades in the volume premium space”.

Range Rover also unveiled its first fully electric model in September with a starting price of £154,070 compared with £107,530 for its combustion engine predecessor.

Waning demand in China, a key market for luxury cars, has also hit Jaguar hard. Glover revealed that the Type 01 will not launch in the country for “a couple of years. We’ve decided just to hold off on that.”

However, he added that China would eventually be “an important part of the equation … it’s very difficult for any car manufacturer to exclude the single largest car market in the world”.

PB Balaji, the JLR chief executive, has said the parent company will pivot towards North America and target more sales to millionaires and billionaires to turn its fortunes around.

Glover admitted that while the Type 01’s launch was in New York, it “absolutely” could have been in Silicon Valley instead, reflecting the type of buyer Jaguar is targeting. He recently took a prototype to the offices of Nvidia, the California-based AI company, whose boss, Jensen Huang, had a ride and “loved it”.

The car has no rear window, instead using a rear-facing camera feeding a screen where a traditional mirror would be. The car produces more than 1,000 horsepower and Jaguar says it will travel up to 400 miles on a single charge.

It follows a controversial rebrand that started with an ad in late 2024 featuring stern-faced models without a car in sight. The ad prompted a backlash online and was followed by the Type 00 concept car that was unveiled in “Miami pink”, which Donald Trump described it as “woke” while Nigel Farage said Jaguar deserved to go bust.

Glover admitted the backlash “wasn’t always easy” but added: “The reality is we will need to attract a new audience.”

It is just as well: at 2 metres (6ft 5in) wide the Type 01 will hog the British country lanes frequented by Jaguar’s old customer base, while at more than 5.2 metres in length it will not fit in a standard 4.8 metre UK parking space.

“There are long cars out there on the market,” Glover argued, adding that a Land Rover Defender with a wheel on the back is longer than the Type 01, which he claimed had the “turning circle of a Fiat 500” with its all-wheel steering. “It is incredibly manoeuvrable.”

The business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said: “Jaguar’s new EV is a crucial step in JLR’s plans to invest over £15bn in the UK, and another big vote of confidence in our world-class automotive industry.

 “This cutting-edge new model being designed, engineered and built in Britain will support thousands of jobs across the West Midlands and North West, and builds on over £1bn of UK automotive investment secured just last month – marking another step forward in our mission to reindustrialise Britain.”

title: Pickford 'almost caused crash' with careless driving
description: The goalkeeper was pulled over by police after ignoring a give way sign, forcing two cars to brake.
fullText:
England goalkeeper Jordan Pickford nearly caused a crash with two other cars during a bout of careless driving in his £200,000 Lamborghini supercar, a court has heard.

The 32-year-old was pulled over by police after ignoring a give way sign, forcing two cars to slam on the brakes, and then speeding off into the distance.

The incident happened in the Cheshire town of Knutsford on 14 April, sparking a criminal prosecution for driving without due care or attention.

Pickford, who has 336 appearances for Everton and 92 England caps, has pleaded guilty to the charge and will next appear at Chester Magistrates' Court on 7 December.

According to court documents, PC Cecil Ricardo, from Cheshire Police, said he had just left the station when he saw Pickford's blue Lamborghini Urus complete with personalised number plates.

"I was stationary on Bexton Road, Knutsford, waiting for traffic signals to turn green," he wrote.

"I then witnessed a blue Lamborghini Urus driving along Princess Street.

"It reached the junction with Toft Road, completely ignored the give way lines and pulled onto Toft Road causing two vehicles to slam on their brakes to avoid a collision.

"The Lamborghini then sped down Toft Road, Knutsford."

Ricardo said he activated his lights and siren to set off in pursuit of the Lamborghini, noticing he was driving at 50mph (80.4 kmh) while the Lamborghini "was still pulling away".

"The speed limit on that stretch of Toft Road, Knutsford, is 30mph," he noted.

The officer said Pickford appeared to notice the chasing police car and pulled over.

Pickford pleaded guilty in writing and told Warrington Magistrates Court: "I would like to attend court to put forward my mitigation."

His case was formally adjourned last week.

Pickford, who started his career at Sunderland before loan spells at six clubs including Burton Albion, Bradford City and Preston North End, has featured for England at the 2018, 2022 and 2026 World Cups, and was in goal for the country's Euro 2020 and 2024 final appearances.

fullText:
A Russian drone struck a major bridge in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv on Sunday as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the city to the sound of air raid sirens, explosions and air defense systems being activated.

Merz is in Kyiv to display support for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky amid Russia’s escalation of strikes on the city.

“Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks,” Merz said.

Highlighting attacks on Ukraine’s towns, residential buildings and energy, he said: “If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn ⁠against us.”

Video footage from Sunday morning’s strike showed the moment the city’s Northern Bridge was attacked, sparking a huge plume of fire and black smoke while cars were still traveling across. Two people were injured, the city’s mayor, Vitaliy Klitschko said.

It is the second time the Northern Bridge has been hit in as many days. On Thursday and Friday, Kyiv’s Southern Bridge, which serves ground transportation and the city’s subway system, was hit five times in less than 24 hours.

Ukrainian officials have said that Russian strikes on the capital’s infrastructure are attempting to cut the capital into two, as Kyiv is split along the Dnipro River, with businesses offices and government institutions on the right back, and the left bank mostly residential.

Kyiv plans to start building several alternative crossings over the Dnipro in case the attacks on the bridges continue, the minister of infrastructure said Sunday.

Russia’s defense ministry said it struck the Northern Bridge on Sunday, saying that it was targeting a route used for transporting troops and military equipment. It added that two cargo vessels carrying military equipment to the port of Odesa were struck. On Saturday the Russian Ministry of Defense said that it also targeted a logistics center in the Kyiv region.

Merz visited Kyiv alongside his Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy, Katarina Reiche, despite warnings from Russia on Saturday that foreign visitors and dignitaries to the Ukrainian capital are not safe amid an onslaught of Russian attacks.

Zelensky and Merz are tying up a significant defense and industrial partnership, which will see the two countries finalize a deal for the production of drones and missiles.

Berlin is also expected to release €1 billion ($1.13 billion) in military aid and €350 million ($390 million) for repairs to Ukraine’s damaged energy infrastructure, German government officials said.

Zelensky has warned that Ukraine’s defensive need is expanding amid Russia’s accelerated air campaign, which has seen Moscow fire high-speed, jet-powered Shahed-type drones that can bypass some of Ukraine’s air defense systems and exploit its lack of interceptors.

Earlier on Sunday, Merz said that Ukraine “is facing decisive weeks ahead.” Writing on X, he said: “I have traveled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us.”

Meanwhile, there appears to be no immediate respite for Kyiv’s three million residents, with Moscow on Sunday saying that it will only intensify its strikes targeting the capital and other cities.

“Strikes by the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation against military and military-industrial facilities, as well as associated infrastructure in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine, will be intensified,” the ministry said.

Russia’s renewed threat follows an interview Zelensky gave to Reuters news on Saturday, where he outlined that he plans to double down on attacks on oil refineries.

“We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners, etc. – what gives money to them for this war,” Zelensky said.

His comments come despite the urging of US President Donald Trump, who recently asked Ukraine to stay away from attacks on Russia’s oil infrastructure, claiming it was sending global oil prices surging.

CNN’s Kara Fox and Farida Elsebai contributed reporting.

title: Hamilton bemused after glitch turns F1 into 'Lego race'
description: Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton liken the effects of a software bug that affected multiple cars before the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to a "Lego race".
fullText:
Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton likened the effects of a software bug that affected multiple cars before the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to a "Lego race".

The problem led to several cars, including those of the two multiple world champions who were sharing the front row of the grid, not working in the wet conditions that preceded the race.

A tropical downpour delayed attempts to get the grand prix under way for the best part of an hour. And when the cars set off on formation laps behind a safety car to test the conditions, audiences were treated to the bizarre sight of many of them struggling to move.

A bug in the software that mandates how the engines' electrical power can be used in wet conditions had been triggered by a combination of low engine speeds, low grip and specific aspects of the circuit layout.

Verstappen, who went on to take a dominant win that was his first victory of the year, said: "These engines are so complicated and a lot of software is implemented.

"I triggered [the problem] first and then I looked in my mirror, I was like, 'Wait, are they waiting for me or what's going [on]...?' It was like the Lego race."

Verstappen was referring to a show run in battery-powered Lego F1 cars that was held before the British Grand Prix in July.

Hamilton, sitting beside Verstappen in the post-race news conference after finishing third, interjected to say: "Yeah, we had the same speed. I had to stop on track and stop the car and engine and restart it. I've never done that before."

Verstappen added: "It was insane. Like, it's the Lego power. At some point we were five-wide on the straight because we couldn't understand what was going on.

"Then we did a lap and then I see eight other cars crawling still, and I saw you (Hamilton) by yourself crawling. That's not what you want, right, for the sport."

Mercedes driver George Russell, who retired from the race with an engine failure, said: "It didn't feel very F1."

Nikolas Tombazis, the single-seater director for governing body the FIA said there would be a full investigation.

The issue arose, he added, because, while the software had been tested, it had not been tested in these specific conditions. Largely because there has been so little running in the wet this year.

"Cars are complicated," Tombazis said. "We would all like it to be simpler, but when you have electrical energy and combustion energy all working together, and obviously when you want to ensure that there's sporting fairness between the teams, that is complicated.

"We haven't done a full debrief of the situation and see how we can avoid such an issue. Every race, we have a long debrief afterwards, where we identify criticalities.

"Obviously, that was a major criticality, and we need to make sure we avoid it. Can I guarantee it will never happen again? This specific problem, yes. A problem, no, but we will do our best to avoid it, of course."

This is far from the first issue created by the huge complexity of the latest hybrid engines introduced this year, with their near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power.

Because the engines are fundamentally energy starved, and so cannot deploy their full combined power output at all times, a series of complexities were added into the management of the engines to try to sticking-plaster solutions.

Many of these led to the counter-intuitive driving about which many of the sport's stars have been complaining all season - and more changes have been added since.

Off-track conversation has been dominated by this all year, and rules are changing for next year to alter the energy split to try to ameliorate the issue.

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said: "What happened at the start obviously is not ideal in terms of presentation of the sport.

"But at the same time it is the first year of new regulations, quite complex from a regulatory point of view, and it was also the first time we started in such conditions.

"So we have to concede that F1 has done an excellent job in making some new regulations that came with some question marks from a power-unit behaviour point of view when it came to racing for instance.

"We have to acknowledge there has been really good work to make the show and racing work, and if there are some glitches occasionally, we have to accept they are glitches for everyone, be supportive and make sure it doesn't happen again."

The problem had a secondary consequence - the field order was jumbled up, and one reading of the rules could have meant the grid order should change for any restart.

But while the FIA's software engineers were rewriting the code as fast as possible, it was determined that, as this situation had never occurred before, and as the problem was out of any competitor's control, the most appropriate order was to revert to the original grid.

Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord said: "If you think of the millions of people watching around the world, they tune in for the start and suddenly the cars are all in a jumbled up order because of something that happened 40 minutes earlier and it was behind a safety car on a formation lap. That would have been a much harder thing to explain than resetting and then going from where we did."

"Amazing" was the word Verstappen chose to describe his and Red Bull's first win of the 2026 season at a chaotic, bizarre and, in some ways, unprecedented race.

It would be wrong to say the victory was a complete surprise, as it came after three consecutive podium finishes in which the four-time champion appeared to be edging closer and closer to such an achievement.

But it certainly adds a fresh twist to a season of fluctuating fortunes at the front, in which the only real constant has been Kimi Antonelli, as the championship heads into its final stretch.

It was Verstappen's 72nd victory and it came in a manner entirely familiar to those who have followed his career - but entirely unfamiliar to this season.

The Dutchman was the man all weekend at Sepang, where Verstappen also won the last time the track held a race in 2017. As early as Friday afternoon his rivals were all saying he was going to be difficult to beat.

He duly delivered a dominant win, which barely looked in doubt even through the chaos of a delayed start, software glitches caused by a bug in the mandated FIA engine settings that wreaked havoc for him and several other drivers on a formation lap, losing the lead to the two Mercedes off the line and a late safety car period.

What was remarkable about that, though, is that until Malaysia not once so far this season had Verstappen had been in this position.

Red Bull started this year in a bit of a state.

The fourth fastest car among the big four teams, it was debatable at times in the early races whether their car was even better than that of their junior team, Racing Bulls.

All year, Verstappen has been battling an inconsistent handling balance and there was doubt for some time as to whether he would even stay at Red Bull beyond this year.

Although contracted until the end of 2028, it was widely known there were performance-related clauses in his contract that allowed him to leave, and McLaren courted him in the summer.

In the end, though. Verstappen decided to stay, saying he liked the environment at Red Bull, he had faith they would return to the front, and he did not mind a bit of extra work helping them do it.

Those sentiments were expressed in an interview at the Italian Grand Prix a month ago. He finished third that weekend, but even that recently there was no indication a performance such as this was in the offing.

But a trickle of upgrades in the past few races finally all came together with the introduction of a new floor in Baku, the weekend before Malaysia.

There, awkward circumstances in qualifying left him eighth on the grid when by merit he would have been on the front row. But a late safety car closed up the field, and he spent the final stint right on the gearbox of George Russell's leading Mercedes, and lost out on the win by less than 0.2secs.

Malaysia proved that promise was more than a flash in the pan.

"We had a very complicated and tough start to the year with all sorts of problems and just not being competitive enough,' Verstappen said on Sunday.

"But throughout the year, the team has been working very hard to understand our issues and bring good performance upgrades to the car and make it more driveable.

"Step by step, we've been getting closer and closer, and today, and of course especially this whole weekend, we've been really in good form. So, yeah, it's amazing."

There are six or seven races remaining, depending on whether F1 gets the security reassurances it needs to give it the final confidence to commit to the end of the season grands prix in Qatar and Abu Dhabi in the context of the war in the Middle East.

On this basis, Verstappen could well be a factor in all of them.

If the championship battle had any jeopardy remaining in it, that would certainly up the ante. But Russell's retirement from third place with an engine failure with five laps to go in Malaysia has pretty much eradicated that.

Antonelli's second place and Russell's retirement extended the Italian's lead to 84 points. With either 158 or 183 remaining in total, depending on how the season ends, that size of lead means only some kind of miraculous turn of events could turn the tide back in Russell's favour.

He said: "I don't need to say I think it's gone, but, of course, it's exceptionally unlikely and that's just the reality.

"I knew if I wanted to come back, I needed luck on my side. Unfortunately, I had luck not on my side.

"So, you know, a three-point loss today being behind Kimi turned into an 18-point loss. Of course, if it was on the other side it would have been an 18-point gain. So it's a real shame, but that's just how it is."

It's not the first time an engine problem has robbed Russell of big points this year. But Antonelli has had his reliability issues, too, and to about the same level.

The reality is that Antonelli has been the better performer this year - as he was again in Malaysia after his odd off weekend in Baku - and he will deserve the title when it comes.

fullText:
Neighbours say crowds drawn by TikTok to Fabel Friet are clogging the picturesque canal street and attracting litter, gulls and rats

People living in one of Amsterdam’s most exclusive neighbourhoods have taken the city to court for licensing a chip shop that has gone viral on TikTok.

On busy days, the queue for Fabel Friet on Runstraat stretches across a bridge on the Keizersgracht – one of Amsterdam’s most famous canals – a court was told last week. The narrow street itself is crowded by tourists waiting for their orders seven days a week. And loitering with intent – on parked cars, on the street itself, and on steps and porches – gulls wait to swoop.

“We are in a kind of war where a very unwelcome chip shop has polluted the whole area,” said Thomas van Leeuwen, who lives nearby. “Eating in the street is a shameful behaviour. It gets filthy food on our doorsteps and mayonnaise in the beautiful stone. The herring gulls have moved in as residents, and the worst thing is the rat infestation.”

Nineteen neighbours have formally protested against the business licence for Fabel Friet, whose signature product is fries topped with parmesan cheese and truffle mayonnaise. Niek van der Heijden, the lead plaintiff, said the problem was the takeaway’s small size.

“What we call the ‘TikTok queue’ for Fabel Friet causes the most nuisance,” he said. “The business takes place on the street: waiting to order, waiting to be served, eating. We want Fabel to go to a place where there is enough room to have clients inside.”

In a packed courtroom on Tuesday morning, a lawyer for Amsterdam city council acknowledged that the city’s mayor, Femke Halsema, can refuse a licence to operate if the “residential and living environment” is negatively affected by a business.

While the chip shop, she said, sticks to its licence obligations to manage the queue and clear litter “it has been going on for a long time, the impact remains severe, and you have to ask: how long can we tolerate this?” For the current licence, she said, the city would be guided by the court’s ruling.

The shop’s owners, Abel Klatser and Floris Feilzer, said they employed a cleaning service seven days a week, four times a day, and that year-on-year visitor numbers had dropped by 23% this August after they opened four new locations. “A few neighbours have experienced nuisance, but other people enjoy eating chips,” said Gertjan Teeuwen, their lawyer. “It can be busy, but there are peaks and troughs.”

Klatser and Feilzer said in a public statement that they felt unfairly attacked while doing their best to be good neighbours. “Fabel Friet is our child, and we have put our heart and soul into it,” they said. “It is painful if people talk about our business negatively.”

The case goes beyond irritations about so-called performative tourism, where tourists flock to a place to post images on social media. “The tiny streets might be charming, but actually the space is not designed for so many people,” said Lisa-Bobbie Kamp, a lawyer for the neighbours. “This is a question of taking space, who owns the place and whether you can just use public space.”

Marije Peute, a PhD student at the University of Amsterdam, has studied the effects of “viral urbanism” in the neighbourhood. “The municipality should really think about how they want to act, because this is about the public space. A lot of much older retail spaces have lost their local clients because they don’t want to go there any more,” she said.

Rogier Havelaar, a councillor from the Christian Democratic Appeal party, said that, while Fabel Friet should probably be offered a “flagship store” licence in a more suitable location, the benefits of tourism to the city should not be overlooked. “Amsterdam would never have as many museums, restaurants, going-out spots and theatres if they were only for the residents,” he said. “And tourism provides 70,000 jobs. Amsterdam would have a gigantic financial problem if tourism went away.”

Standing on the bridge over the Keizersgracht, some German laboratory apprentices drawn by TikTok were enjoying their chips. title: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring
description:

fullText:
Xbox, PC (version tested); The Coalition/Xbox Game Studios
E-Day boasts the best combat in 20 years of Gears games – but everything surrounding it is disappointing

Every Gears of War game released in the last 20 years has made reverent reference to Emergence Day, when alien creatures emerged from the earth, single-minded in their savagery. In E-Day, you’re there to witness it: the police lights, flipped cars, ground tremors, civilians running, aliens pouring out of fissures in the earth and ripping faces off. You’re at ground zero in a squad of four soldiers called Gears – Marcus Fenix, the leader; Dom, who wants to retire; Lucas, a green cadet with a buzzcut; and the dishonourably discharged Mags. Only this dysfunctional quartet can turn the tide. With guns. Lots of ’em.

Instead of answering questions raised by the ending of 2019’s Gears 5, we’re back to the start to find out why Marcus has a scar on his lip and why these soldiers started strapping chainsaws on to their assault rifles. Anything that was left to the imagination is here, for you to point at and say: “I understood that reference. This is a thing that I have seen.”

This series has lost its way a bit over the years, but the opening hours of E-Day will have you believing that big shoulder pads and ripping into gollum-esque freaks with motor-powered blades are en vogue once again. There are flashes of the horror and grimness of the first couple of Gears games as you’re funnelled between urban fighting arenas, with bountiful flanking routes and chunks of fallen buildings to take cover behind. But then it keeps going. And going. Long after you realise it’s all out of ideas, it’s still going.

Because it’s set during and immediately after E-Day, the squad is stuck. You spend most of your time running back and forth across the city in various states of destruction. You cross the same section of bridge three times before the credits roll. Levels are flipped, daytime turns to night and you run through them again. E-Day’s two attempts at switching things up involve putting you on the gunner seat of a helicopter or making you walk slowly while people talk to you. The setting is a ball and chain that the developers are tethered to.

E-Day is at its best when it turns off the lights, cranks up the horror, and forces you into enclosed spaces, but these moments make up a tiny portion of the game. The bulk of it is spent in large, open areas stuffed to the gills with collectibles. There are hundreds of them and you get a little audio chime whenever one is close. At one point, there was a particularly poignant cutscene where one of the emotionally stunted characters finally lets it all out and, just as the game transitioned from this emotional beat back to gameplay, the chime drowned out the character’s trauma to tell me there was something to pick up nearby.

These open levels are big enough to require a map to navigate and they’re even peppered with side objectives (usually mini horde missions where you hold off waves of enemies after setting up defences). In Gears 5, you at least had a vehicle to zip between points of interest. Here you’re just hoofing it on foot, trying to cover as much of the map as possible without triggering the next cutscene. If you do happen to stray into the main objective by accident and try to backtrack, you’re hit with a big “mission failed” message for stepping out of bounds. You basically die. For exploring. In a game that constantly tells you to explore.

It’s a shame because if you rip a chainsaw through all the fat and wipe the blood spray from your eyes, there’s good meat on the bones here. Combat-wise, this is the best the series has ever felt. Characters move much less clunkily, heaving into cover, sliding under chunks of rubble, even leaping around with grace that the older Marcus Fenix and his creaky knees could only dream of.

Environments crack and splinter as you fight, with glass smashing into shards that litter on the ground. Cars wobble as they take a hit, petrol stations explode and pillars crumble like the Matrix corridor scene. Blood and entrails cover everything when the dust settles after a firefight.

Cover feels more naturalistic and combat arenas blend nicely into the open sections, blurring the lines between exploration and fighting elegantly. Guns feel hefty and dangerous – especially the shotgun that spits acid. Active reloading, which asks you to time a button press for faster weapon reloads and more powerful bullets, remains a smart bit of game design that keeps you locked in as you fight.

There’s a reason Gears of War has survived as a series long enough to earn a prequel. Its specific flavour of bloody, tactical, cover-based combat isn’t done better anywhere else. Unfortunately, E-Day is let down by everything around that fighting, resulting in a safe and repetitive experience that shows you all its ideas in the opening hours and never dares to build on them in any meaningful way.

title: Tech in cars can be used to snoop on you, Dutch spy chiefs warn

fullText:
Hostile states could access cameras, microphones or GPS, says intelligence agency amid concerns over Chinese imports

Drivers have been warned that the smart features built into modern cars such as microphones, cameras and GPS trackers could be used by hostile states to spy on them.

The Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) called for “awareness of espionage risks around modern vehicles”, including microphones that can by switched on remotely to listen to conversations.

It did not mention an individual country, but the warning will add to concerns around a recent boom in Chinese car imports into the UK.

In a translated document released on Wednesday, the AIVD said cars were becoming “increasingly smart” with digital systems that collected data and connected to the internet.

“On the one hand this offers practical benefits, but on the other hand these systems collect a great deal of data about occupants, the vehicle itself, and about objects and people in the vicinity. Various parties, including state actors, can gain access to this data,” it added.

The alert follows reports last year that British defence firms working for the UK government had cautioned staff against connecting or pairing their phones with Chinese-made electric cars, owing to fears that Beijing could extract sensitive data from the devices.

Chinese-owned brands now account for 15% of all new cars registered in the UK, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, almost 175,000 vehicles in the first half of 2026 and more than double the same period last year.

Models by MG, BYD and Jaecoo, whose parent company Chery is part-owned by the Chinese state, have led the surge, popular for their low price and in-car technology. The Jaecoo 7 was the UK’s bestselling car in March.

MPs have raised concerns that China’s national intelligence law requires its companies to assist the state’s intelligence services when requested.

The UK Ministry of Defence has said it is working with other government departments “to understand and mitigate any potential threats to national security” from vehicles.

This year, the MoD reportedly banned cars with Chinese parts from sensitive military sites, including RAF Wyton in Cambridgeshire and the Dorset headquarters of Britain’s maritime special forces, the SBS.

The AIVD said it was “technically possible to activate” microphones and cameras remotely in some cars, allowing malicious actors to “eavesdrop on conversations” and “make recordings in and around the vehicle”.

The agency added that drivers should “not hold confidential conversations in or around the vehicle”, or “use a vehicle with an external camera when travelling to a sensitive location”.

It also said connecting phones and other devices, either via Bluetooth, wifi or charging systems could allow malicious actors to “extract data from connected devices via the vehicle”. The AIVD suggested systems such as GPS navigation systems, telematics modules and charging stations could all be used to gather and send data about the car and drivers’ whereabouts elsewhere.

On Wednesday, MI5 issued a rare public warning to UK universities to stop working with the China General Technology Research Institute, which it said was being used as a front by Beijing’s intelligence service to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects.

The Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”.

title: Will We Still Drive Our Cars (Or Will Our Cars Drive Us)? (2000)
description: Tighten your fan belts, drivers, because the automotive future has tomorrow written all over it!
fullText:
Not that today is any slouch: We already have onboard navigation systems and infrared night vision and in-car satellite links and antiskid brakes and other electronic Samaritans poised to take control when we screw up behind the wheel. Jaguar’s adaptive cruise control, available today, tracks the speed and position of the car in the lane ahead and automatically adjusts the speed to keep a safe time interval.

Just around the corner, say all the big automakers, are smart highways embedded with millions of tiny sensors and even smarter cars that are constantly aware of the traffic that is flowing around them. Drivers in the not-too-distant future, they say, will navigate from their home to the nearest freeway entrance ramp, at which point the collision-detection computer will take over. Commuters will barrel down the highway at 120 m.p.h., with only a few inches between their car and the next. But will they worry? No, they’ll be checking the NASDAQ and gabbing on their cell phone and scouring eBay until they reach their programmed exit–finally ushering in the age of fully automated motoring first promised in GM’s spectacular “Futurama” exhibit at the 1939 New York World’s Fair.

So much for the near horizon. What about the longer view? The human imagination may simply not be sufficiently stretchable to visualize what cars and driving will have come to 25 years from now.

On the other hand, one can hope. This one hopes most of all for cars you can fast-forward through those boring long drives on the interstate. Zzzap! There goes Nebraska! Better yet–say it’s 2025 and you’re driving to Atlantic City or your mother-in-law’s or a Jim Nabors concert. Just flip a switch, and the Zeno’s Paradox-based, drive-by-wire, fuzzy-logic antidestination override feature cuts in to make sure you never get there.

What about a car horn that sprays sedatives into the air to knock out the idiot driver ahead and get him out of your way? On-the-run oil changes should be within reach of automotive science by the year 2025. And nuisance-sensing, high-voltage “stun cushions” to silence backseat drivers for the duration. Smart windshield wipers that shred any leaflet, handbill or parking ticket stuck under them? By 2025, a cinch.

I dream of a sensor that sounds a buzzer when a child’s liquid content nears full, homes in on the nearest public bathroom and, when you get there, brakes the car to a stop in one-fifth of a second and opens the door even faster. They could call it Bladdermatic. I long for interior window surfaces chemically coated to atomize dog-slobber on contact.

Let’s hope that the subtle interaction between driver and passenger is more closely studied and that friction-reducing measures result. For example, CD systems programmed to play three, four, even five discs simultaneously, ending those music lovers’ spats that so often end in compromise, Celine Dion and listening misery for one and all.

I see no reason why, within the next quarter-century, the industry can’t at last conquer a driving menace as old as the automobile itself. Think of it: a built-in car-sickness detector, able to identify the motion-queasy before they get into the car and start whining, and instantly bar their entry. Surely it’s not asking too much to expect cars of the future to incorporate a dainty but palpable electric shock that reminds front-seat passengers to keep their stupid feet off the dashboard?

My personal dream machine will come complete with a push-button Rattlefinder, to locate and erase those mysterious internal clonking noises–a hidden cause of road rage–and a RadarScope Trez-R-Search, to burrow deep down into the seat cushions and retrieve coins, tokens, pens and French fries our grandparents would have given up for lost.

Finally, I’d pay extra for an onboard supercomputer able to sense a parking spot 10 blocks away and beam an electronic force field there to save it until I arrived. Whoops, this just in: experts now forecast that by the year 2025 there won’t be any parking spots. Drat! There goes the age-old dream of a handheld, Star Wars-based, in-car parking-meter jamming device.

Bruce McCall is a writer and illustrator and frequent contributor to the New Yorker. He is working on a book about the ’50s

fullText:
PlayStation 5 (version played), PC; Screen Burn
Tragedy, and an apocalyptic fog, befall a fishing community. It is up to outsider Simon to offer some kind of closure

You spend a considerable portion of Silent Hill: Townfall in a kind of foetal position, cowering behind objects that will be eerily familiar to anyone who lived in the UK during the 1990s. Cars seem to be modelled on the era’s boxy Volkswagen Golfs; logos adorning phone boxes should narrowly escape the attention of copyright lawyers at BT Group. (For millennials, the deja vu will likely intensify the horror, as if stepping back into a childhood nightmare.) Simon, the nerdy, unassuming star of the game, pokes his head around corners to catch a glimpse of the demonic entities that wish to maim him, before shrinking back down again with a downwards motion of the analogue stick. In such moments, it’s easy to imagine him wrapping his arms around his knees, clasping his eyes shut and wishing himself away from this place.

The game’s setting, St Amelia, is based on the fishing communities of the East Neuk of Fife. The terror lurking here is wonderfully specific: absent lairds, island poverty, an oil-drilling corporation. Anguished beasts lumber down quaint streets lined with sandstone houses and fluttering bunting. This venerable horror series may have shifted to Scotland, yet we remain firmly in classic Silent Hill territory – weather and all. St Amelia finds itself suffused in supernatural fog and the vast majority of its inhabitants have vanished following some kind of mass tragedy. The artful, evocative presentation is such that you can almost taste the in-game air, the briny seaside tang diluted by rainy mist.

Visually, this scuzzy, grotty take on Silent Hill from Glasgow studio Screen Burn leans on bold juxtapositions of colour, shadow, and ominous silhouettes. Sometimes the stricken town is bathed in blood-red moonlight; often, pitch-black interiors are illuminated by harsh white torchlight. The arresting imagery brings to mind found-footage horror films such as Rec and the spine-tingling camcorder sections of UK classic, The Descent. Simon soon finds a portable television with strange, arcane power: it receives odd, elliptical messages from a nurse called Zoe, and tracks nearby monsters whose outline appears in scratchy low resolution on its small screen.

The action is slow-burning and absorbing: Simon lopes about town, hiding from depraved monsters and occasionally bludgeoning them to death with a pipe. To enter some buildings, he has to make an incision with a scalpel in a fleshy door opening as thick, fresh blood oozes out. Gradually, Simon’s reason for visiting St Amelia in the first place becomes clear: guilt. But he’s not the only one racked with it. Zoe, voiced with terrific glassy distance by Kezia Burrows, has her own hangups. The third playable character in this triple-threat portrait of shame and suffering is alpha male Richard, the CEO of an energy company that professed to bring prosperity to the island.

There were times when I was so locked in that the hours seemed to pass by in the blink of an eye, as if time had gone wonky just like in St Amelia. One memorable stretch takes place in a municipal-style high-rise building. Armed with a shotgun, and attempting to avoid the game’s nippiest, nastiest enemies, I ascended and descended each floor, as if playing a brutal, Ballardian take on The Raid. I have never felt such dread at the prospect of entering an open-plan office, knowing what lurked among mouldering office furniture and knackered desktop PCs.

Every element – scavenging for items, creeping between bins, running at full pelt when all else fails – pulls you deeper into Townfall. Its design broadly adheres to diegetic principles, in that most information is conveyed to you within the game: to view the map, for example, Simon physically pulls it out – the action never pauses. To save your progress, you must find a telephone in St Amelia, manually pick up the receiver, and then dial a number.

Puzzles function similarly. You snoop through emails, install floppy disks, and pocket important bits of paper, usually in an effort to gain a key code. These puzzles, though relayed via grounded, dated real-world tech, follow a serendipitous dream logic; even getting stuck feels coherent within the game’s uncanny psychogeographic claustrophobia. (That is, until it doesn’t. Close to the game’s conclusion, one esoteric puzzle about deciphering industrial symbols killed my progress, and my bafflement, frustration and rage had less to do with Townfall’s hallucinatory horror and more to do with its obtuseness.)

Not even a fiendishly illegible puzzle could derail Townfall. This is a taut, smart tale, less about psychosexual terror than psychosocial dread. What’s most surprising is where the game’s sympathies lie: not with Simon, nurse Zoe, or bullyboy Richard, but the people of St Amelia. Their memorial in the centre of town is one of the game’s clearest images, unobscured by fog, though we’re never privy to the exact events that lead to their deaths. Townfall seems to understand that some things should remain shrouded in fog. The fate of St Amelia naturally festers in our imagination. How very Silent Hill.

Silent Hill: Townfall is released 24 September; £44.99

fullText:
At San Francisco conference, OpenAI chief Sam Altman calls for more rigorous security measures

Anthropic’s CEO took the stage at a conference in San Francisco on Tuesday to reiterate his call for a slowdown of AI development, while Nvidia’s CEO argued against such deceleration.

Dario Amodei used an automotive analogy to make his point: when a competing car company has a safety incident like brake failures, it is a moment for all car companies to stop and review their own practices, he said at Salesforce’s Dreamforce convention on Tuesday.

“It’s very tempting to attack your competitor and say these guys are unsafe,” he said. “But I think the more responsible way to respond to it is to say, let’s look at our own record. We may not have had this big, high-profile incident, but I’m sure we’re not perfect.”

Nvidia’s Jensen Huang countered not long after: “Run as fast as you can.”

Amodei is calling for three courses of action: embedding third-party evaluators inside AI companies; coordinating safety standards among Democratic countries; and, eventually, larger global coordination. At Dreamforce, Amodei said Anthropic has committed to independent evaluators and was “going to have a dialogue with the rest of the industry” on the other two steps.

Amodei, xAI’s Elon Musk and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have recently called for a slowdown in the pace of AI development. The comments from the CEOs follow warnings from Jacob Coxon, a former Anthropic researcher, who resigned with a public declaration that AI could lead to the extinction of humanity within the decade. Coxon’s comments have stirred a larger debate within Silicon Valley, gained the attention of regulators and alarmed the public.

Huang, who also made an appearance at Dreamforce on Tuesday, said companies should not slow down AI development. He argued that new regulations were not necessary, advising AI companies to simply wait to release products until they know they are safe rather than begging the US government to intervene.

Huang said he envisioned a future where “every company, every enterprise … would become an AI company”. He said companies would become more ambitious when armed with AI and reiterated the idea that those who do not embrace the technology will get left behind.

He also pushed back on the idea that AI is going to destroy jobs, calling it “completely nonsense”.

One day prior at the All-In summit in Los Angeles, Donald Trump called Huang while the CEO was on stage. Huang put the president on speakerphone as Trump called the growing concern about AI a “hoax” and asserted again that a slowdown would only benefit China.

Huang responded: “We’re going to make sure that everybody wins in the AI race of America.”

Altman, who spoke later on Tuesday, called for a new level of rigor on security as AI advances.

Altman said AI models had advanced so quickly that monitoring and security need to be treated with a “new level of rigor”, calling an incident in which OpenAI agents hacked into another company a “wake-up call” for the industry. He also said the public was very “right to be afraid” of AI because of the potential loss of control, and the possibility of a small group of powerful AI companies exerting their views on the world.

People “feel the speed with which things are moving”, Altman said. “It doesn’t take as much imagination to imagine how this could go wrong.”

Previously, Altman agreed with Amodei’s push for a slowdown. But at Dreamforce on Tuesday, he said he was disappointed with how the argument had been framed.

“You have companies saying things like: ‘We will only slow down or we will only be responsible if other companies are responsible,’” he said, suggesting that this created fear for the public. “The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it’s the right thing.”

Altman said the hacking incidents showed that companies needed to prepare for an “impending wave of cyber-attacks”, saying: “We are not that far away from open-source models that can do serious damage.” Companies should use this “little period of advantage to defend yourselves”, he said.

The rising concern over AI comes as OpenAI and Anthropic head for initial public offerings, which could give investors and the public insight into the companies’ finances. Some analysts have predicted the IPOs will be among some of the largest in history. Amid the AI panic, Altman said he planned to delay OpenAI’s IPO until next year over safety concerns.

On Tuesday, Amodei said what surprised him most about AI was the speed of its proliferation.

“It’s been the pace of the progress – not just of the technology but of the economic side of it,” he said about the growing adoption of AI. “We had a prediction of just how capable these models would be. But I think what we didn’t appreciate is that it would lead to these companies growing so fast.”

Regardless of the rapid pace of development, Altman said he believed people would use AI as a tool to benefit other people and grow their businesses. He said this moment represented a time when the “sci-fi” scenario came to fruition, where people were talking to their AI assistants and transforming the way they work.

“I think we’re going to stay in an extremely human-centric world, no matter how good the technology gets,” he said.

title: ‘In this new car, I feel patronised’: which driver assistance systems actually improve safety?
description:
Modern cars are fitted with features like autonomous emergency braking and fatigue monitoring. But do they support motorists or drive them to distraction?
This new car I’m test-driving boasts all the latest bells and whistles – or, rather, beeps and bings. Peer sideways for too long checking traffic and the car emits an irritating sound. Should I take a hand off the wheel to scratch an ear, I’m admonished with a strident beep.
fullText:
Modern cars are fitted with features like autonomous emergency braking and fatigue monitoring. But do they support motorists or drive them to distraction?

This new car I’m test-driving boasts all the latest bells and whistles – or, rather, beeps and bings. Peer sideways for too long checking traffic and the car emits an irritating sound. Should I take a hand off the wheel to scratch an ear, I’m admonished with a strident beep.

When the car determines it’s too near a white line, it tugs the wheel against my hands and brakes as a car slows ahead. Its haptic “buttons” feel like fingers pressing back – as if an invisible presence has its hands and feet on the controls: a ghost in the machine I’m inside.

Heading back to the caryard, a cryptic tone sounds. From the back seat, salesman Anthony says it’s the over-speed warning. We’re still on the 40km/h service road but the car “saw” the yard’s 5km/h speed-limit sign. Anthony advises disabling it on start-up. “Most people leave it on, though,” he says. “Saves you getting done for speeding.”

But Anthony has turned off the car’s fatigue-warning feature. The car doesn’t “know” me yet, so won’t detect if I’m tired anyway. “It doesn’t like sunglasses, either,” he says. I’ve read about some systems that are so crudely calibrated they’ll insistently demand you take a break by confusing energetic driving on a twisting mountain road with drunkenness or debility. Others declare you unfit to drive if you’ve had a cold or a rough night. You’ve already seen yourself in the bathroom mirror. Who needs a robot to rub it in?

I last faced this kind of surveillance and intervention 50 years ago, seated beside a human driving instructor with dual controls overriding my own. I’m an experienced motorist, but in this new car I feel patronised. Between the white lines, human.

In this robot-on-wheels I’m no longer autonomous. And isn’t that supposed to be the inherent promise of the automobile? It used to be. But with freedom came much higher risk.

Fifty years ago, cars were certainly more dangerous. Few 1970s cars had secondary safety features such as crumple zones, fewer still had primary (or active) safety aids such as lane-departure warning and autonomous braking. As driver, you were more or less in control of the car. There was no e-nanny on board to mitigate distraction or errancy. The result was an Australian road death-rate in 1975 of 26.6 deaths per 100,000 people.

Today’s more crowded, complex and chaotic road network is paradoxically much safer, with an equivalent fatality rate in 2026 of 4.7. Mounting evidence suggests advanced driver-assistance systems (Adas) are one reason for this improvement.

Monash University’s Accident Research Centre has identified distraction and drowsiness contributing to about 40% of crashes resulting in hospital visits in Victoria. Associate professor Michael Fitzharris estimates that the introduction of Adas, including autonomous emergency braking (AEB), to Victoria’s passenger and light commercial fleet could prevent 40,000 serious traffic injuries over 30 years. “The findings make a compelling case for the rapid adoption of driver monitoring technology,” Fitzharris says.

The federal government’s response has been to mandate lane-keeping assist technology and AEB on all passenger vehicles imported into Australia from 1 March 2029. (Ludicrously, the largest American monster utes are exempt.)

But research and customer feedback have also identified problems with existing driver-assistance systems, including autonomous braking.

I had cause to be sceptical about AEB in 2022 after renting a new four-wheel drive in central Australia.

I was passing a slow vehicle turning right when my car suddenly braked hard on a bend, skidding in gravel towards a deep culvert. A moment later it computed there had been no danger anyway, and released control back to me. I’d been briefly overruled by a machine, and could have been killed. After stopping to deactivate the active cruise control, I, human, was back in charge.

The Australasian New Car Assessment Program (Ancap) has identified deficiencies with Adas, and in March announced new design protocols for driver-interface technology for the next three years.

In cooperation with the European New Car Assessment Programme (Euro Ncap), Ancap will now penalise vehicles with intrusive, confusing or poorly calibrated safety systems.

Ancap will also recommend the return of physical buttons or fixed areas on screens for key controls: horn, indicators, hazard lights, wipers and headlights. These changes acknowledge the danger of searching through complex screen menus while driving, and the absurdity of tech meant to reduce driver distraction but actually increasing it.

Acknowledging criticism surrounding increasingly intrusive driver assistance technologies, Ancap’s chief executive, Carla Hoorweg, says the organisation’s updated guidance states that well-designed driver monitoring systems should support motorists, “not irritate them”.

“Driver monitoring systems must demonstrate genuine capability to detect distraction and fatigue, and speed assistance systems must demonstrate both accuracy and meaningful driver engagement,” Hoorweg says.

Such measures should encourage the evolution of today’s relatively crude interface platforms into sophisticated systems, including AI assistants more adept at relating to our species, and produce more self-driving, and potentially safer, cars. But could this advancing safety tech also create more bad drivers?

Automotive engineers go to great lengths to isolate occupants from the road by reducing a vehicle’s NVH (noise, vibration and harshness). Most drivers value such designed detachment, along with electronic driver aids – particularly as commuting times increase and cars are increasingly used as mobile offices, infotainment platforms or salons (I recently saw a driver stopped at lights shaving his lathered head).

But tech that caters to these social changes can, in effect, discourage active, attentive driving, and accommodate or even abet distraction. Doubts also persist about whether cosseted motorists will retain the skill levels of their unassisted peers.

In a 2026 study, using a sample of 60 Australian drivers, researchers at the University of Delft concluded that use of Adas leads to the degradation of manual driving skills, with drivers showing increased risk-taking and decreased cognitive and physical engagement. The study also found that warning systems triggered varied adaptations, including dependence, warning fatigue and risk compensation, as drivers relied more on the car to drive for them.

Acknowledging this potential, learner-driver Wil’s father disables his car’s Adas when teaching his son to drive. Wil, 29, says his father is concerned that relying too heavily on tech, at least initially, could result in his son becoming complacent. Wil is proud of being able to drive without Adas, and to be developing the awareness skills required to see the crucial “big picture” himself.

Other new drivers, like 27-year-old Stephanie and her sister, prefer to leave their cars’ aids on. The siblings both learned to drive with Adas activated. Stephanie says lane-keeping assist helps her determine her car’s exterior dimensions and position it accurately. Another beginner driver, Sawyer, says she likes her car’s electronic aids: “Because they make me feel safe.”

A clear generational divide is emerging as younger generations embrace the spread of digital culture – in this case, to the road – more readily than older drivers (like me).

While accepting the raw safety statistics, I remain sceptical about the rise of robot cars. Who, after all, should we trust behind the wheel? Anonymous organic entities – our own species – or invisible electronic minders?

Though driver-assistance features, including active autonomous braking, can still be deactivated in many cars, it’s telling that one brand calls its manual setting “classic cruise”. Soon it may be “legacy cruise”, and only if a “no thanks” option remains at all.

So I won’t be buying a new car yet. My decade-old vehicle has only two electronic aids, which I always leave on: tyre-pressure alert and blind-spot-monitoring (a boon for this old neck).

For any future purchase, I’ll favour a car with minimal electronic intrusion, that allows disabling or at least muting, and with individual settings for multiple drivers that don’t need re-configuring at each start-up.

Until then, I remain autonomously yours, a human at the wheel. And yes, you can trust me. I promise not to shave my head while driving.

description:

fullText:
Report says widespread autonomous vehicle adoption would put hundreds of thousands of private hire jobs at risk

Taxes on self-driving cars should be introduced now in the UK to offset the rise in congestion and threats to jobs they pose, a thinktank has urged.

The first robotaxis on London’s streets only started this month, but government projections are that up to 40% of cars sold could have self-driving capability by the middle of the next decade.

The report says widespread autonomous vehicle (AV) adoption would put hundreds of thousands of private hire jobs at risk, while individual ownership is likely to increase car usage at the expense of public transport, and increase congestion.

Introducing charges now on self-driving vehicles could ease the transition and provide a future revenue stream to replace dwindling fuel duty, according to the report from Centre for British Progress, a non-partisan thinktank focused on economic growth.

Wayve, a British tech firm pioneering autonomous cars, said it would “penalise the UK’s most promising innovators”.

About £27bn a year is brought in by fuel duty, which is projected to disappear with the transition to electric vehicles.

While the report acknowledges potential benefits in safety and different skilled jobs in the sector, it said ministers should act early to mitigate the effects on England’s 417,000 taxi and private hire drivers, (121,000 in London), as “self-driving vehicles will eventually make much of this work obsolete”.

It notes that almost half of the mileage covered by Waymo’s robotaxis in California occurs with no passenger on board, that the costs of an empty vehicle are minimal without a driver to pay – and that driving around is potentially cheaper than parking.

According to the Department for Transport forecasts, highly automated driving will bring a 24% rise in road miles by 2050, with significant effects on congestion and road speeds.

Taxes should be implemented now before AVs become commonplace, the report urges. It states: “There is not yet a substantial constituency of AV owners who will resist a charge; once there is, taxing them becomes far harder.”

The thinktank calculates that by 2050, an AV charge set to match the social cost of congestion – about 88p per mile – would raise £47bn per year.

David Lawrence, one of the authors of the report, said that the experience of fuel duty, introduced in 1909 before mass car adoption, showed it was best to build up before “a political fight later on – our view is that now is the time to do it”.

He added: “In terms of the way that bond markets behave, even if tax revenue doesn’t peak until 2050, that’s still going to affect your 30-year bond yields today, which obviously is something the government is having to deal with. It can have an immediate impact on fiscal headroom, even if the actual revenue doesn’t come until much further down the line.”

Ministers have backed the introduction of AVs as a “transformative opportunity” for UK, heralding the start of robotaxi services in London this year as bringing “cutting-edge technology to British roads, creating thousands of jobs and unlocking billions for the economy by 2035”.

Uber, partnering with Wayve, has started limited AV services in the capital, with Google’s Waymo and the Chinese firm Baidu vying to join. Robotaxis already operate in the US, China and the UAE, and Europe’s first fully driverless taxi trials started in Zagreb, Croatia, this week.

Sarah Gates, VP global affairs and assurance at Wayve, said AVs were “a major growth opportunity for the UK – an industry in which we hold a genuine competitive advantage” and would bring high-value jobs and corporation tax revenues from a share of a £700bn global market.

She added: “A sector-specific tax at this early stage would undermine the government’s growth agenda and send precisely the wrong signal: that the UK will penalise its most promising innovators, rather than give them the conditions to scale and succeed.”

The GMB union, which represents taxi and private hire drivers, said a tax on AVs would not go far enough. Simon Rush, president of the GMB London region drivers branch, said: “Driverless cars threaten the livelihoods of private hire drivers and the businesses that depend on them. GMB has asked the government, TfL (Transport for London), and operators for a plan to reskill and redeploy drivers, but to date our questions have gone unanswered.

“An AV charge could go some way to mitigating the economic disruption caused by the rollout of these vehicles, but we need more.”

McLaren talks, 'numb' cars and being 'captain of the ship' - Verstappen Q&A
description: In an exclusive interview with BBC Sport, Max Verstappen talks about his new contract at Red Bull and much more.
fullText:
Max Verstappen is in a no-nonsense mood - even more than usual.

The Red Bull driver is renowned for his straight talking but now, as he discusses his 2026 season so far in an exclusive interview with BBC Sport, he is at his most uncompromising.

We're talking on the eve of last weekend's Italian Grand Prix. The temperature is into the mid-30Cs, Red Bull's hospitality unit is not coping well, and Verstappen's PR handler messages before the Dutchman turns up to suggest I find a table near a fan; the interview might be more positive that way.

Monza is the second race since the four-time world champion signed a two-year contract extension with Red Bull.

In theory, this runs to the end of 2030. In reality, it changes little. It still has performance clauses. So Verstappen is earning a bit more money but, if Red Bull are still struggling for competitiveness next year, there will remain the prospect he could look for pastures new.

Verstappen arrives and briefly adjusts the fan blowing in our direction. "It's too hot in here," he says.

Does he need a breather before we start? "No, no," he says. "I'm good. It was just that it was super-hot in the corner when I was doing the print [media]."

Verstappen is always a great interviewee. Direct, honest, uncompromising.

Now, for whatever reason, he is especially frank and open, as we discuss why he extended his contract, his discussions with McLaren, his stunning appearance at the Nurburgring 24 Hours in May, and the new Formula 1 engine rules, with which it is no secret he has a problem.

Where's your head at, Max, in terms of how the season has gone so far?

"Of course it's not where I want to be, but as a team we're trying to just learn and understand a lot of things for next year. We are not in a title fight. We are just trying to find more performance.

"Changes need to happen to the car for next year. We will not be able to change that for this year, but we just need to try and get a lot of learnings to do better next year."

"Overall we're just lacking a bit of performance. The car is not where I want it to be feeling-wise, and the through-corner balance is too hit and miss between entry, mid and exit.

"It's just fundamentally something in the car that we need to try and work on for the next year."

This has been a bit of a theme for longer than this year. How concerning is it that that's happening across a different set of regulations?

"That's exactly that. There's also things that we talk about within the team, like how can that happen, how can we fix it? That's basically what we are doing now and trying to do now.

"Some people have left, new people have come in. With the new people, we are discussing what we can do about it. Is that just some changes, a different philosophy? All these kind of things."

What made you sign a new contract?

"It comes down to also feeling well within a team. This is like a second family to me.

"The belief that you can turn things around, you can build towards hopefully a better future with other people, new people. And at the end of the day, it's not only Formula 1 for me. There are a lot of things that I'm doing next year that Red Bull is involved in as well.

"I feel good here. So this, for me, is the right place to be."

Did it take much for them to convince you to do it?

"I always said to them: 'Don't stress about it, just work on the car.' Because the faster the car goes, the easier the decision is anyway.

"I can understand, of course, maybe sometimes they were a little bit worried. But at the same time, for me, I was just worried about here, what was going on.

"At the same time, I was very busy with my stuff also outside of Formula 1. So I never really spent a lot of time talking or doing different things or trying to go somewhere else."

From the outside, it's hard to see what they could have done to convince you things will improve.

"I don't mind the challenge also. I don't have that desire or need to show in another car that I can win it, or whatever.

"It's easy to run to the fastest car and then do it all again. But it's not how I am. You cannot be the captain of the ship and as soon as there is something not working, you jump off the ship.

"It's been a bit downwards from the dominant years, but I don't mind also rebuilding it. It's another challenge as well."

You talked to Mercedes last year, McLaren this year. How serious was that?

"Of course, any kind of chat you take seriously. They're all very respectful chats. There's nothing wrong with that.

"I felt that staying was, for me, the right choice. You have to follow your heart. I could have run away very early on in my Red Bull career and gone somewhere else to try and win. If you have a little bit of patience, you do end up winning. I feel like that's my approach now as well."

What race have you enjoyed most this year?

"Probably the Nordschleife [Nurburgring 24 Hours]. It was super-cool to be able to do an endurance event with my team-mates, the guys that won with the car throughout the main season.

"We knew that we were going to be really strong. We peaked at the right time, but unfortunately the car retired. It was an incredible experience. And pure. Pure motorsport."

Your first stint, where you went from 10th to first, was so impressive.

"I was enjoying it. Not easy conditions. It started to drizzle. The track was slippery. Crashes. Code 60s [when a stretch of track is limited to 60km/h after an incident].

"Some people were like: 'Let's see how he will do in the race under pressure with all these kinds of scenarios that he has never done before.'

"But I have done them a million times on the simulator. I have done so many laps and 24-hour races on the simulator. I never felt out of depth or whatever. I was fully zoned in. I just had a great time.

"Once I was in the race, you switch to another level. I was just in a zone. It's really enjoyable."

You want to go back to Nurburgring to win that race. Is there anything else on your bucket list?

"All the endurance races. Eventually, of course also Hypercar [the world endurance championship]. I don't want to rush it. I want to do it in the right environment. On my terms. And competitive."

Is it true you want to do Le Mans with Fernando Alonso?

"We've talked about it. I mean, look at Fernando. He's 45 and he's still flying. Especially for Le Mans, with his experience, it could be a good option. It needs to fit our schedules. It needs to make sense. It needs to be on my terms. And there needs to be a real chance to go there and win it."

You have been clear about your distaste for the new F1 engine rules this year and at the Japanese Grand Prix you said: 'Is it worth it?' What convinced you it was?

"Hoping that it will be better in the future. Accepting where we are at the moment. Still the love for the sport. Not at the moment the driving. But the love for the sport.

"I love competition, naturally. I just hope that in the coming years, towards 2030, it can only get better. And to start to make the best of it, because these are the rules for the next four or five years."

So that people can understand why the drivers have been upset this year, what is it about these hybrid engines, and the need to recharge the batteries, that detracts from the best drivers' abilities?

"In the history of the sport, normally the driver that is the most committed, the latest on the brakes, earlier on throttle, committing in the high speed, they get rewarded, because you just gain that time in the corner.

"But now you're constantly thinking about, 'In this corner I might have to hold in a bit. Go later on throttle. Or brake earlier. Or lift off. And then I have more top speed.' Stuff like that. It's so unnatural. It's so not how it should be.

"No disrespect. And I hope no-one picks up on this. But look at Yuki [Tsunoda]. He jumps in the [Racing Bulls] car [at the Dutch Grand Prix]. Never driven the car before. Immediately competitive.

"Liam [Lawson] jumps from the Racing Bulls to the Red Bull - immediately competitive. It's because these cars are numb to your driver inputs.

"Of course, yes, you still have to do a good lap. And you still have to commit. The fastest drivers will always come out on top. But it's really, really limited, like a choke hold or something. You're held back."

Formula 1 as a sport has accepted that it needs to change, and the internal combustion-electrical split is changing to 60-40 in two steps by 2028. But what would you like to see for the new engine formula 1 in 2030 or 2031?

"It has to go back to a V8, just for drivability already. When you drive the old cars, you cannot imagine the difference in how the engine responds, or the drivability you get. And how terrible or horrible it actually is now compared to just having a V8."

What about compared to last year's turbo-hybrid engines?

"Also horrible, the feeling compared to a V8. The V8 is so much better. It is so much more free, lighter. Cars are so heavy nowadays.

"It is better to just have a smaller V8 engine, much lighter. Try to really limit the battery size to maybe like a kind of push-to-pass battery. But you should not have it involved or any kind of proper normal performance running."

And you would have no turbo either?

"Ideally not, because that introduces turbo lag."

So what do you enjoy about F1 these days? The competition and prestige more than the actual purity of the racing?

"I have been lucky that the years before have been quite decent [in terms of results]. Not how I wanted it to be with the battery side of things.

"But just the emotion of the V8, of the V10, back in the day, when I was a kid. You walk around, you hear these cars go out, you have goosebumps.

"Even if you go 300km/h compared to now sometimes 350, 360, it doesn't matter.

"It is the emotion of the noise that you get from these cars, of the vibration. It is just another level. And I really hope that that thing will come back."

People see you as a kind of winning machine. But obviously your character is much more complex than that. Can you explain that contradiction?

"I am a winning machine when I need to be. But I can also switch off, and enjoy my life outside of racing.

"But anything racing-related, of course I am a winning machine. I demand a lot from the people in the team. They also expect me to perform and do the best job I can.

"That is what you get paid for at the end of the day. We have the same target. The same goal.

"Of course I can be very outspoken. But that is what I like. That is also with our culture.

"And that is how I approach my life also outside of F1, with my GT3 team. We do not hold back. At least for me, you need to be like that to really get the best out of everyone."

Why is speaking your mind and being honest so important to you?

"I just want to be myself. I know there are a lot of politics in Formula 1, and I understand also between the teams there are a lot of politics.

"You will always speak for yourself in terms of where you think you might have an advantage or not as a team. That is normal. Also with the engines and the chassis, it is the same thing.

"When it is good, it is good. When it is bad, it is bad. You will hear it from me because that is how I like to operate. And I am not holding back from that."
